title: A Clever Trick and a Kept Oath
overview: A nearby people fools Israel into a peace treaty to escape destruction, and Israel's leaders keep their sworn promise even after learning the truth.

parts.label: Kings join forces (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The city-states across Canaan were usually rivals, but after Jericho and Ai fell they agreed to fight Israel together. This sets up the battles in the next chapters.

parts.label: A disguise from Gibeon (vv. 3-6)
parts.note: Gibeon was a large town about six miles northwest of Jerusalem and roughly 18 to 20 miles from Israel's camp at Gilgal, close enough for Israel to reach it on the third day of travel. Its people dressed as worn-out travelers, with moldy bread, cracked wineskins (goatskin bags for drink) and patched sandals, to look as if they came from far away.

parts.label: Why distance mattered (vv. 7-13)
parts.note: Israel's law forbade treaties with the peoples living in the land but allowed peace with distant towns, so the visitors kept insisting they lived far off. They mention what God did in Egypt and east of the Jordan but say nothing of Jericho or Ai, as if that recent nearby news had not reached them.

parts.label: A deal made in haste (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: Israel's leaders inspected the food but did not ask the LORD for guidance, which the writer clearly presents as the mistake. They then swore an oath of peace, promising to let the Gibeonites live.

parts.label: The oath holds (vv. 16-21)
parts.note: Within three days Israel learned the truth, and the people grumbled, but the leaders refused to break a promise sworn in God's name. Much later, 2 Samuel 21 tells of King Saul breaking this oath and a famine following, which shows how seriously it was taken.

parts.label: Spared but made servants (vv. 22-27)
parts.note: The Gibeonites admit they lied because they had heard Israel was told to wipe out the land's inhabitants, and they feared for their lives. Joshua spares them and assigns them permanent work cutting wood and carrying water for the community and the LORD's altar, an arrangement the text says still stood when it was written.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the Gibeonites should be seen mainly as people who genuinely turned toward Israel's God and found mercy, much like Rahab, or mainly as deceivers whose trick exposed Israel's carelessness.
think: If someone lied to you because they believed their life depended on it, how much would that change the way you judge the lie?
